<reason>Side B built a stronger path to victory by successfully defending the binding timetable against feasibility and equity attacks. While Side A raised powerful pressure about credibility (the hold-vs-waive dilemma) and uncompensated costs to developing nations, Side B effectively neutralized these with the phase-in structure (newbuilds first, gradual retrofitting), the port-state-control enforcement mechanism, and the weighing that climate devastation costs the poor far more than fuel premiums. Side B also convincingly argued that Side A's alternative intensity standard lacks a guaranteed endpoint and fails to break the coordination deadlock that only a binding fuel mandate can solve. Side A's rebuttals were sharp, particularly the distinction between binary mandates and continuous carbon pricing, but could not fully defeat Side B's case that the proposition as written is both necessary and workable.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange occurred in Rebuttal 2, where Side A's A1 sharply distinguished binary fuel mandates from continuous carbon pricing to answer the verification inconsistency charge, but Side B's A1 on phase-in (newbuilds complying immediately while existing tonnage transitions gradually) successfully preserved the binding timetable's credibility by demonstrating it need not demand instant global fuel availability, thereby defusing Side A's strongest credibility dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
